item.title: Derivatives market gets Gen Z twist, but losses cast a long shadow: Sebi
item.description: Around 89 per cent of traders below 30 were loss-makers in FY26 compared to 81 per cent of participants above 60 ...
item.dc:creator: Press Trust of India
item.content:encoded: The country's equity derivatives market has taken on a notably younger profile, with traders under 30 making up 43 per cent of individual participants in FY26, a sharp rise from 31 per cent four years earlier, according to a study.However, the younger cohort also recorded a higher incidence of losses, the study by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) revealed.Around 89 per cent of traders below 30 were loss-makers in FY26 compared to 81 per cent of participants above 60.The changing age profile is part of a wider transformation in the retail derivatives market, which has increasingly drawn investors outside India's largest cities and from relatively lower-income groups.About three-fourths of individual derivatives traders belonged to the annual income category of below Rs 5 lakh. This group accounted for 43 per cent of turnover, but 53 per cent of aggregate losses, the regulator said.Around 88 per cent of traders in this income category incurred losses, compared with 81 per cent of investors with annual income of above Rs 1 crore.The geographical spread of derivatives participation has been equally striking.Investors from smaller towns (B30) accounted for about two-thirds of individual traders and nearly half of derivatives turnover in FY26.The study noted that B30 investors account for only about one-fourth of individual mutual fund assets, pointing to a markedly higher derivatives risk appetite relative to their broader investment behaviour.The study also examined the relationship between derivatives trading and the size of investors' underlying equity portfolios.In FY2526, around 95 lakh, or 78 per cent, of individual derivatives traders had equity portfolios below Rs 1 lakh.This group accounted for 51 per cent of turnover, but as much as 70 per cent of aggregate losses.The study also found that traders with equity portfolios below Rs 1 lakh, but derivatives turnover above Rs 1 crore, represented only 13 per cent of traders, though accounted for 52 per cent of aggregate losses.Around 43 lakh traders, or 35 per cent of individual derivatives participants during FY25-26, had no underlying equity portfolio at the end of FY26.This indicated participation in derivatives without any cash-equity holdings.The study also found that the overall individual trader base contracted 18 per cent, from 1.06 crore in FY25 to 87.5 lakh in FY26.Sebi's analysis examined how trading outcomes varied with age, income, location, trading activity and portfolio size, while cautioning that these relationships should not be interpreted as proof of causation.

item.dc:creator: Tamal Bandyopadhyay
item.content:encoded: What do the State Bank of India, HDFC Bank Ltd, Bank of Maharashtra and DCB Bank Ltd have in common? Well, all four, and, for that matter, all listed Indian banks – both private and government-owned – have less than 1 per cent net non-performing assets (NPAs) in the June quarter of FY27.

item.title: Panama-flagged cargo ship sinks in Bay of Bengal, 22 crew members missing
item.description: A Panama-flagged cargo ship carrying iron ore fines from Odisha sank in the Bay of Bengal, leaving 22 crew members missing.
item.dc:creator: Hemant Kumar Rout
item.content:encoded: Twenty-two seafarers went missing on Sunday after a Panama-flagged cargo ship MV Ocean Winner carrying over 72,000 tonnes of iron ore fines from Odisha sank in the Bay of Bengal, around 230 nautical miles off the eastern coast, according to officials. Two of the 24 crew members aboard the vessel MV Ocean Winner have been rescued from life rafts so far, while an intensive search-and-rescue operation is underway to trace others. En route to China, the 225-metre vessel sailed from Paradip Port on August 21 after loading iron ore fines. The crew members included 20 Chinese, three Myanmarese, and one Bangladeshi. The Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre (MRCC) at Sri Vijaya Puram (Port Blair) activated the search-and-rescue (SAR) response after communication with the vessel was lost. Coast Guard ships - Varad, Anmol and Vijit and a Navy maritime surveillance aircraft have been deployed, while merchant vessels operating in the vicinity have also been alerted to assist in the search. “MRCC Sri Vijaya Puram initiated a swift SAR effort following a distress alert and loss of contact with MV Ocean Winner, nearly 230 nautical miles south-east off Paradip. Diverted via international safety net, MT AISOPOS successfully rescued two survivors from life rafts,” Indian Coast Guard (ICG) said in a statement. The ICG has since intensified the operation to locate the remaining crew members. Indian Navy is coordinating with the coast guard to locate the missing crew members. The rough conditions in the Bay of Bengal, however, are making the search increasingly challenging. “The two rescued crew members are from China. They are now in the rescue ship and will be brought to the mainland. Search operation is underway to rescue others,” Commandant Amit Uniyal, a spokesperson for the Coast Guard, told Business Standard. Though the precise circumstances that led to the ship losing communication and subsequently sinking have not been established yet, the vessel sank within 8 to 10 minutes after it began to tilt permanently to one side. Authorities are examining whether the incident was linked to weather and sea conditions, cargo-related issues, mechanical failure, or any other factor. The vessel’s disappearance from tracking systems before sinking will likely be taken up for investigation. Union Minister for Ports, Shipping and Waterways Sarbananda Sonowal has expressed concern over the incident. He said: “Deeply concerned by the unfortunate incident involving MV Ocean Winner off the coast of Odisha. The Panama-flagged vessel was carrying iron ore from Paradip port to China,” in a social media post. Sonowal said all agencies are coordinating closely and actively conducting search and rescue efforts. Two survivors, who have been rescued so far, are being given medical care. Their rank and identity are currently being verified, he added, wishing for the safety of the remaining crew. MV Ocean Winner was reportedly built in 1998 and has a deadweight capacity -- a measure of the total weight a ship can carry -- of nearly 72,928 tonnes, while the cargo loaded at Paradip port was about 72,200 tonnes. One of India's largest ports for handling bulk commodities, Paradip port is a major gateway for iron ore, coal and other mineral cargo, with large international bulk carriers regularly sailing through the Bay of Bengal after loading at its berths. The sinking of the China-bound cargo vessel brings back memories of earlier maritime accidents, including the one involving MV Black Rose. This Mongolian-flagged vessel carrying nearly 23,847 tonnes of iron ore and around 920 tonnes of furnace oil had sunken only a few kilometres from Paradip port after developing a hole in its hull in September 2009. The Black Rose incident was followed by another close call when the Vietnam-flagged MV Vinalines Mighty developed a serious stability problem while carrying about 24,500 tonnes of iron ore from Paradip port. The vessel reportedly began tilting and sent an SOS, although a major disaster was eventually averted. In 2009, MV Asian Forest suffered a similar fate. It had loaded iron ore fines at Mangalore Port on India's west coast and capsised due to cargo liquefaction.

item.description: Shareholder approval clears a regulatory hurdle as Swiggy prepares an inventory-led qcom model that could boost reported revenue, margins and operational control ...
item.content:encoded:
Home / Companies / News / Swiggy gears up for inventory-led qcom model after shareholder nod

Swiggy gears up for inventory-led qcom model after shareholder nod Shareholder approval clears a regulatory hurdle as Swiggy prepares an inventory-led qcom model that could boost reported revenue, margins and operational control

Image: Bloomberg

Udisha Srivastav New Delhi 4 min read Last Updated : Aug 23 2026 | 7:22 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Earlier this month, shareholders of food delivery and quick commerce (qcom) company Swiggy approved resolutions to become an Indian-owned and controlled company (IOCC) at the firm's annual general meeting (AGM), clearing a key regulatory hurdle for its planned shift to an inventory-led qcom model.

Analysts expect the operational transition to begin from Q3, with Swiggy having already begun key groundwork, including talks with brand partners, inventory planning, and changes to its operational dashboard.

“From Q3 onwards, they will start with an inventory model and the margin benefit is likely to emerge over the subsequent two quarters," said Shobit Singhal, research analyst at Anand Rathi Institutional Equities, who added that Swiggy has been preparing for the shift for the past two-three months.

The change carries weight well beyond operations. An industry source said marketplace operators typically report only the commission they earn, while inventory-led platforms record the full value of the sale. With commissions usually running at 20-35 per cent, the source estimated Swiggy's reported revenue could rise four to five times once the shift takes effect, depending on the product mix.

Experts, however, caution that the shift is less dramatic operationally than the regulatory language implies. Also Read

“Business looks at an inventory model, meaning a brand has sold inventory to the (qcom) platform, and the platform is controlling it largely and selling it to the market,” said Nishant Shekhar, managing director and partner at Boston Consulting Group.

By his estimate, more than 90 per cent of qcom operations already function as inventory-led from a business standpoint — the marketplace format is mostly confined to newer categories with less predictable demand. The regulatory distinction still matters, though, because it determines legal ownership of the inventory.

What Blinkit's year already shows

Since no other qcom player has made this transition, Blinkit — which moved to the inventory model a year ago — is the only real precedent, and its numbers give a sense of the trade-offs Swiggy is signing up for.

Eternal, Blinkit's parent, said in its Q1FY27 results that it had completed a full year as a first-party business. The company has since raised its steady-state capex estimate per dark store, including warehousing, to ₹2.5 crore from ₹1 crore — a bill Swiggy should likely expect, too.

In exchange, net order value per store per day has risen to ₹11 lakh from ₹7 lakh, reflecting larger stores, wider assortment and more efficient warehousing — the kind of payoff Swiggy will be measured against. Working capital has also become more efficient, with net working capital now estimated at 12 days of NOV (3.3 per cent), down from 18 days (5 per cent) — a gain that could help offset the higher capex.

Margins, market share, and the case for control

Datum Intelligence founder Satish Meena expects Swiggy's transition to take three-four months, likely rolling out city by city or store by store, with sellers no longer needing to handle their own GST registrations as Swiggy absorbs that back-end work. Meena said the real impact will show up in margins, but Swiggy may choose to reinvest the savings in dark stores, discounts and market-share gains rather than let them flow straight to profit: “Swiggy finds this is a very good time for acquiring market share from Zepto.”

Ravi Kapoor, partner and retail sector leader at PwC India, said the case for inventory extends beyond margin maths. “The shift towards inventory-led models is driven not only by compliance requirements but also by the need to deliver a more consistent and reliable consumer experience,” he said, noting that direct control over inventory improves assortment, pricing and availability, and — because inventory can then be distributed more widely across dark stores — fulfilment speed, too.

The marketplace model isn't going away entirely, though. It remains useful for testing smaller brands and new categories, since unsold inventory doesn't sit on the platform's books — and as those categories mature and demand becomes predictable, platforms have an incentive to eventually fold them into the inventory model. Industry experts expect both models to run in parallel, depending on category and supply-chain maturity.

For Swiggy, then, the real test isn't the regulatory label itself, but whether it can match Blinkit's operating gains while absorbing a capital requirement that has proven far steeper than initially expected.
